title: Social Media Hashtag Standards in Emergencies
html:
Today, I am happy to share publicly the OCHA Think Brief entitled Hashtag Standards for Emergencies, which was developed in collaboration with Roxanne Moore and Qatar Computing Research Institute (QCRI).

 

What does the paper recommend?

Essentially, we suggest that governments or response agencies develop a strategy and promote the adoption of standard hashtags to be used in an emergency.  More specifically, we advocate the following three hashtag categories:

  1. Disaster title hashtags. This type of hashtag (e.g. #Sandy) would be used by anyone to generally comment on an emergency (e.g. Hurricane Sandy) and would not be actively monitored by response agencies.
  2. Public reporting hashtags. By suggesting a specific hashtag that citizens can report non-life-threatening emergency items they see (e.g. #311US for broken power lines or a damaged bridge in the USA), we would be making sensors of the entire population. The resulting data could be scanned, mined and filtered to the relevant responding agencies.
  3. Emergency response hashtags. By providing a standard hashtag to trigger emergency response, based on local standards (e.g. #911US for the USA), we would enable citizen to tag content that is absolutely critical.  It would also enable responders to set up dedicated social media monitoring tools and channel the  resulting information into their already existing mechanism(s). Social media would become an official information source.

By separating the standardization into these three categories, we aim to make machines and humans better able to monitor and filter social media messages into the appropriate channels for relevant action.  It begins to make big [crisis] data more manageable.

A little history on how the paper came about

In early 2009, I set up a rudimentary monitoring dashboard in TweetDeck watching for mentions of certain country names and hashtags.

In 2010, with the recognition of the growing importance and relevance of using Twitter to gain situational awareness, I drafted a paper for OCHA to consider the benefits of suggesting standard, unique hashtags during emergencies - similar to the concept of unique Glide Numbers. Although it did spark some discussions, including the consideration of automatic hashtag issuance, the idea was slow on the up take.

Since that same time period, OCHA has been working with groups like the Digital Humanitarian Network, Qatar Computing Research Institute (QCRI), Standby Volunteer Task Force, Humanity Road, GISCorps and ESRI Disaster Response to scrap public Twitter messages, filter them into relevant categories, and produce a variety of online and offline products. Although extremely manual in the first few collaborations, everyone began to recognize the benefits of being able to look through such big data sets. But we needed a more efficient way to scan, filter and allow volunteers to tag the content.  With that in mind, OCHA began collaborating with QCRI to build out solutions such as AIDR and MicroMappers as technical solutions to aid these challenges.

In May 2014, in recognition that any “full” solution meana that both a technical and policy approach is needed, Ms. Gwi-Yeop Son (OCHA) and I visited Dr. Abdellatif Saoudi and Dr. Patrick Meier of QCRI in Doha where we discussed the need to draft a policy paper that urges the promotion of standardized hashtag by governments and/or response agencies (pre-disaster) as well as encouraging anyone posting to enable GPS when sharing public data.

Around the same time, the Philippines Presidential Communications Development & Strategic Planning Office (PCDSPO) shared their Report on Standard Hashtags for Disaster Response based on their experience in Typhoon Yolanda (Haiyan). Essentially it talks about the policy success (of standard hashtags), but the technological failure (how to handle, filter and respond).

From June this year, Roxanne Moore and I, with great input from QCRI, set about to draft Hashtag Standards for Emergencies. It was published as an OCHA Think Brief on 4-Nov-2014.

Andrej

FYI: just in the past week, it was announced that twitter will become another source of information for the Philippines official emergency response mechanism….where standard hashtag monitoring will obviously be critical.
